abstract: Peter McCrory, Head of Economics at Anthropic, synthesizes roughly 18 months of Anthropic economic research into a framework for why generative AI has not yet raised US unemployment. His argument has three parts. First, the US labor market is currently stable and near maximum employment: June unemployment of 4.2%, a vacancy-to-unemployed ratio just above 1, a prime-age employment-to-population ratio near multi-decade highs, and stably low initial claims. Second, the AI sector is now large enough that macroeconomic effects should be detectable - roughly 20% of firms use AI in at least one business function (40% in the information sector, 5.5% of GDP), and quality-adjusted AI output grew over 2,000% per year in both 2024 and 2025 - and McCrory argues those effects are showing up in productivity rather than unemployment, with labor productivity growth of 2.0% per year from 2022Q1 to 2026Q1 versus 1.6% in the four pre-pandemic years. Third, the reason unemployment has not moved is that AI so far behaves as a skill-biased, labor-augmenting technology: no O*NET occupation has all of its tasks systematically handled by Claude, complex Claude outputs correlate with sophisticated human inputs, and agentic coding shows persistent returns to human expertise even as the return to straightforward implementation falls. He is explicitly hedged about the future, noting that model capabilities are advancing rapidly, that the jagged frontier may smooth, and that automating innovation itself could produce very different dynamics.
keyFindings: No material AI-driven increase in the US unemployment rate to date, including among workers in occupations highly exposed to current patterns of AI automation. Updating the Massenkoff-McCrory labor impact analysis with more recent BLS data does not change the result.

Hiring rates for young workers in highly AI-exposed roles have weakened somewhat over the past year, consistent with Stanford Digital Economy Lab's Canaries findings - but McCrory argues this should be read with caution.

The central alternative explanation offered for early-career weakness: from 2022 to the present the US experienced the largest non-recessionary labor market slowdown on record (the 'immaculate disinflation'), producing a 'low hire, low fire' labor market that hits early-career entrants hardest for reasons unrelated to AI.
Software engineering job postings have broadly rebounded since May 2025 relative to all other postings - rising demand in the occupation where AI capability gains have been largest.

Weak-links evidence on software production: a 10-20x increase in lines of code generated after the introduction of coding agents yielded only a 30% increase in software releases, and no total increase in app usage.

Approximately 20% of US firms use AI in at least one business function; 40% in the information sector, which is 5.5% of GDP. Quality-adjusted AI output grew over 2,000% per year in both 2024 and 2025 (McKelvey and Korinek).

Labor productivity growth ran 2.0% per year from 2022Q1 to 2026Q1 versus 1.6% in the four years before the pandemic, and sectors with higher AI adoption have had faster labor productivity growth. Total factor productivity growth has been more modest, which McCrory concedes weakens the evidence.

No job in the O*NET taxonomy has all associated tasks systematically handled by Claude. Non-automated tasks - interpersonal coordination, in-person interaction, engagement with the physical world - both constrain the productivity lift and amplify returns to labor.
Workers in roles with tasks Claude is used to automate express greater concern about job loss than those in less exposed roles, even though their unemployment rates have not risen.

In the June 2026 Cadences report, over a third of Anthropic Economic Index Survey respondents expect AI to handle most or all of their job tasks within twelve months, and a similar share expect job responsibilities to change - but expectations of actual job loss were notably lower.

Across quits, layoffs, and job-finding rates the pattern is stability, with no evidence of unusually fast AI-driven occupational churn. Since firms hire on beliefs about future match value, McCrory treats this as evidence that firms do not currently expect AI to devalue new hires.
methodology: Not a primary research paper. This is a long-form essay published as an X article on 22 July 2026, originally circulated internally at Anthropic, synthesizing published work by the Anthropic Economic Research team and outside researchers. The evidence base it draws on includes: the Anthropic Economic Index reports (Economic Primitives, January 2026; Learning Curves, March 2026; Cadences, June 2026), the Massenkoff-McCrory labor impact report updated with more recent BLS data, the 81,000-user Claude productivity survey, the Claude Code agentic-coding expertise analysis, Stanford Digital Economy Lab's Canaries in the Coal Mine, McKelvey and Korinek on quality-adjusted AI output, METR task-horizon results, BLS productivity and employment statistics, JOLTS-derived vacancy ratios, the NY Fed Heise-Pearce-Weber Labor Market Tightness Index, and BLS occupational projections through 2034. The theoretical frame for the closing section is the weak-links growth argument of Aghion, Jones and Jones (2017): essential tasks that resist automation constrain aggregate growth and can keep the labor share elevated even under rapid but incomplete automation.
qualifiers: Tier 4: an X post by an interested party. McCrory is Head of Economics at Anthropic, writing about the labor market effects of a technology his employer builds and sells, and the essay's evidence base is drawn overwhelmingly from Anthropic's own research using Claude conversation data. The post carries a 'views are my own' disclaimer. Essentially every quantitative claim is a restatement of a source already independently registered in this corpus, so the essay should be read as interpretation rather than new measurement - its distinctive contribution is the macro-confound argument, not the underlying numbers. McCrory is candid about the limits of his own case: total factor productivity growth has been more modest than labor productivity growth, which he concedes 'weakens the evidence'; he calls the displacement evidence 'mixed' before saying he is 'unconvinced'; and he flags that isolating AI from the post-pandemic unwinding, rapid monetary tightening, commodity volatility, trade-policy uncertainty, and the post-pandemic rise in remote work is genuinely hard. He also states plainly that the labor-augmenting property may not persist: 'It may very well be the case that the skill-biased, labor-augmenting aspect of AI will go away as models continue to improve. The jagged frontier may become smoother. And at a certain point, the returns to human expertise may diminish.' His forecast horizon is explicitly one year. Note also that the macro-confound argument cuts both ways: a 'low hire, low fire' labor market could equally mask AI displacement that shows up in hiring rather than separations, a possibility the essay does not address.
